title: Structuring a full-stack feature from the start
what: A feature is easier to maintain when its browser, API, business and persistence responsibilities are separated clearly.
how: Define the user flow first, then the API contract, backend use case, persistence model and frontend state boundaries. Keep each layer responsible for one kind of decision.
code:
React page
  -> feature hook
  -> API client
  -> Controller
  -> Service
  -> Repository
  -> Database
delivery: I start from the user capability and trace it through each boundary. That keeps the feature cohesive without putting backend rules into React components or UI concerns into services.
followups: How do you organize packages by feature?
traps: Do not put business rules directly in React or controllers.

title: Designing a full-stack CRUD feature
what: CRUD connects React forms and lists to Spring Boot create, read, update and delete endpoints.
how: Model each operation explicitly, return useful HTTP statuses, validate input on the server and reconcile React state from authoritative responses.
code:
GET /api/products
POST /api/products
PUT /api/products/42
DELETE /api/products/42
delivery: I design CRUD around clear resource semantics and make the server authoritative. React manages interaction and presentation while Spring Boot validates and applies business rules.
followups: How do you handle optimistic updates?
traps: Do not treat a successful HTTP request as proof that the UI state is already correct.

title: Mapping DTOs between React and Spring Boot
what: DTOs define the data contract exposed by Spring Boot instead of leaking persistence entities to the browser.
how: The controller accepts request DTOs and returns response DTOs. The service maps them to domain or persistence models and controls which fields are exposed.
code: CreateOrderRequest -> OrderService -> OrderResponse
delivery: I keep the API contract independent from the JPA entity model. That prevents database changes from accidentally becoming frontend breaking changes.
followups: Should response DTOs contain nested entities?
traps: Do not serialize JPA entities directly just because it is convenient.

title: Building a React form backed by Spring validation
what: A production form needs immediate browser feedback plus authoritative server validation.
how: React validates obvious client-side constraints for UX. Spring validates the request DTO and returns structured field errors. React maps those errors back to the relevant controls.
delivery: Client validation improves responsiveness, but server validation remains authoritative because requests can be created outside the browser.
followups: How do you model validation errors?
What status should validation failures use?
traps: Never rely only on browser validation for security or correctness.

title: Implementing pagination end to end
what: Pagination prevents large datasets from being transferred and rendered at once.
how: Spring Boot accepts page and size or cursor parameters and returns the requested slice plus pagination metadata. React keeps page state and renders navigation based on that metadata.
code:
GET /api/orders?page=0&size=20

Response: { items: [...], page: 0, size: 20, totalElements: 137 }
delivery: I make pagination a server-side concern for large datasets and keep the frontend responsible for navigation and display state.
followups: How do you keep sorting stable?
traps: Do not fetch every row and paginate only in React for large datasets.

title: Building search and filtering across the stack
what: Search and filters should be expressed as API parameters so the database can do the expensive filtering close to the data.
how: React debounces user input and sends normalized query parameters. Spring validates parameters and builds an efficient query with stable sorting and pagination.
code: GET /api/orders?status=SHIPPED&query=truck&page=0&size=20
delivery: I push filtering to the backend when datasets are large and keep the frontend focused on collecting filters, debouncing and presenting results.
followups: How do you index the filtered columns?
traps: Do not create a new request for every keystroke without considering load and cancellation.

title: Handling authentication across React and Spring Security
what: Authentication establishes who the user is and lets the frontend display the right session state while Spring Security enforces identity on the server.
how: The browser obtains a session or access token through the authentication flow. Requests carry the required credential, and Spring Security validates it before protected controllers execute.
code:
Login
  -> credential validation
  -> authenticated session/token
  -> protected API request
  -> Spring Security
  -> Controller
delivery: I keep identity enforcement on the backend and let React reflect the authenticated state for UX. The browser is never the final authority.
followups: Where should access tokens be stored?
traps: Do not consider a hidden React route to be authentication enforcement.

title: Implementing protected routes and protected APIs
what: A protected frontend route controls navigation, while a protected Spring endpoint enforces actual authorization.
how: React checks the current authentication state and redirects unauthenticated users. Spring Security checks authentication and authorities for every sensitive API request.
code:
React route guard -> /admin
Backend -> GET /api/admin/orders -> requires ADMIN
delivery: I use frontend route protection for user experience and backend authorization for security. Both layers have different responsibilities.
traps: Never trust a role stored only in React state.

title: Designing a consistent API error contract
what: A consistent error response lets React handle validation, authorization, conflicts and unexpected failures predictably.
how: Spring Boot maps exceptions through a global handler into a stable structure containing status, code, message, field errors when applicable and a trace identifier.
delivery: I define an error contract as part of the API contract. React can then translate known error codes into deliberate UI states instead of parsing arbitrary server messages.
followups: What should be exposed to users?
How do you correlate the error with logs?
traps: Do not expose stack traces or internal exception messages to browsers.

title: React handling 401, 403, 404 and 409 responses
what: Different HTTP failures require different user experiences and recovery actions.
how: 401 usually means authentication is missing or expired, 403 means access is denied, 404 means the resource is unavailable, and 409 indicates a business conflict that may require reconciliation.
code:
401 -> refresh/login
403 -> show access denied
404 -> show not found
409 -> show conflict/reload
delivery: I map HTTP status categories to explicit UX behavior rather than showing one generic error for every failure.
traps: Do not retry every non-2xx response blindly.

title: Implementing optimistic updates safely
what: Optimistic updates make the UI feel fast by showing an expected result before the server confirms it.
how: React updates local state immediately, sends the mutation, and either keeps the result on success or rolls back using the previous state when the server rejects the change.
code:
previous = cache
update UI optimistically
POST /api/orders/42
error -> restore previous
delivery: I use optimistic updates only when rollback is well defined. The server response remains authoritative and failures must be visible.
followups: What if two users edit simultaneously?
How do you prevent duplicate mutations?
traps: Do not optimistically show an irreversible action as successful without a recovery path.

title: Handling file uploads from React to Spring Boot
what: File uploads require multipart requests, server-side validation and a storage strategy.
how: React builds FormData and sends multipart/form-data. Spring receives the multipart file, validates size and type, stores it in an approved location or object store, and returns a safe identifier or URL.
delivery: I validate uploads on the server and avoid trusting the filename or MIME type supplied by the browser. Large files should usually go to object storage rather than the application filesystem.
followups: How do you generate download URLs?
traps: Do not execute or serve uploaded files from an unsafe location.

title: Managing transactions in a full-stack order flow
what: The browser request can initiate a business transaction, but the database transaction boundary belongs on the backend.
how: Spring service logic performs the required database changes inside a transaction. React waits for the business result and displays success or a recoverable failure.
code:
POST /api/orders
  -> @Transactional service
  -> order + order items
  -> commit
  -> 201 response
delivery: I never try to coordinate a database transaction from React. The backend owns transaction boundaries and returns a business-level result.
followups: What if an external payment call fails?
traps: Do not keep a database transaction open while waiting on a slow external service unless there is a strong reason.

title: Preventing duplicate submissions
what: Users can double-click a button, refresh, retry a request or lose the response after the server has already processed it.
how: Disable or debounce the UI for immediate feedback, but enforce correctness with a backend idempotency key for operations that must not execute twice.
code:
POST /api/payments
Idempotency-Key: 7f3e...

Repeated request -> same business result
delivery: Frontend measures reduce accidental duplicates, but the backend must enforce idempotency because duplicate requests can originate anywhere.
followups: Where is the idempotency key stored?
How long should it be retained?
traps: Do not rely only on disabling a React button.

title: Handling concurrent edits from multiple users
what: Two users can read the same resource and then attempt conflicting updates.
how: The backend can use optimistic locking with a version field or conditional update. React handles a conflict response by refreshing or asking the user to reconcile changes.
code:
PATCH /api/orders/42
If-Match: version-7

409 Conflict -> resource changed
delivery: I detect concurrent changes at the server boundary and make the conflict explicit to the frontend instead of silently overwriting another user's update.
followups: When would you use pessimistic locking?
traps: Do not assume the last request to arrive should always win.

title: Caching full-stack data correctly
what: Caching can reduce latency and database load, but stale data must be handled deliberately.
how: Spring can cache suitable read operations, while React can cache server state on the client. Mutation paths must invalidate or update affected data consistently.
code:
GET /api/products
React cache -> Spring cache -> DB
POST /api/products -> invalidate relevant caches
delivery: I define cache ownership and invalidation rules before adding caching. A cache is useful only when its staleness behavior is acceptable.
followups: What data should never be cached?
traps: Do not add caching without deciding how stale data is reconciled.

title: API versioning when frontend and backend deploy separately
what: Independent deployment means old and new clients can temporarily call different versions of an API.
how: Use backward-compatible changes where possible and version breaking contracts explicitly. Keep compatibility windows long enough for active frontend clients to migrate.
code:
/api/v1/orders
/api/v2/orders

Old frontend -> v1
New frontend -> v2
delivery: I prefer additive API changes first and explicit versioning for genuine breaking changes. The goal is to avoid synchronizing every frontend and backend deployment.
followups: How do you handle renamed fields?
traps: Do not remove an API field immediately after deploying a new frontend.

title: Generating and using OpenAPI contracts
what: An API contract documents endpoints, schemas, validation and responses so frontend and backend teams share the same expectations.
how: Spring Boot can expose an OpenAPI specification. Frontend tooling can use the specification to generate types or clients, reducing hand-written contract drift.
code:
Spring controllers
      -> OpenAPI spec
      -> generated client/types
      -> React
delivery: I treat the API contract as a shared artifact. Generated clients are useful when the organization values strong consistency between backend changes and frontend integration.
followups: How do you detect breaking changes?
Would you generate a full client or only types?
traps: Do not assume documentation is accurate if it is maintained separately from the API implementation.

title: Testing a React feature against a Spring Boot API
what: Full-stack confidence comes from testing both UI behavior and API behavior without making every test depend on the entire production stack.
how: Use component tests for UI behavior, backend integration tests for HTTP and persistence behavior, and a smaller number of end-to-end tests for critical user journeys.
code:
React component test
+ Spring MockMvc/integration test
+ critical browser E2E test
delivery: I use the testing pyramid: fast isolated tests for most behavior, integration tests for boundaries, and a focused set of end-to-end tests for critical flows.
traps: Do not make every frontend test a slow end-to-end test.

title: Testing the API contract between React and Spring Boot
what: Contract testing checks that the frontend's assumptions about API requests and responses remain compatible with the backend.
how: Define expected request and response shapes and verify them in CI. Breaking changes are caught before incompatible versions reach production.
code:
Frontend expectation
  <-> API contract
  <-> Spring implementation
delivery: I use contract tests when frontend and backend evolve independently. They protect the integration boundary without requiring every test to exercise the whole system.
followups: How do you handle optional fields?
traps: Do not test only that an endpoint returns 200; verify the contract that clients depend on.

title: Managing environment configuration safely
what: React and Spring Boot need environment-specific configuration, but browser configuration is public while backend secrets must remain private.
how: Expose only non-sensitive frontend configuration at build or runtime. Keep credentials and private connection details in backend environment or secret-management systems.
code:
Frontend: VITE_API_BASE_URL=https://api.example.com
Backend: DB_PASSWORD=<secret manager>
delivery: I classify configuration by exposure. Anything shipped to the browser should be considered public; secrets stay server-side.
traps: Never put a database password or private API key into a Vite client variable.

title: Dockerizing a React and Spring Boot application
what: Containers provide repeatable packaging for the frontend and backend runtime environments.
how: Build the React application into static assets served by a web server or CDN, and package Spring Boot as its own container. Configure networking and environment variables at deployment time.
code:
React build -> static web server
Spring Boot -> JVM container
Both -> deployment network
delivery: I keep frontend and backend artifacts independently deployable unless the deployment platform strongly benefits from a combined image.
traps: Do not bake environment-specific secrets into container images.

title: Using a reverse proxy for a full-stack application
what: A reverse proxy can serve frontend assets and route API traffic to Spring Boot services behind one public origin.
how: The proxy serves static files for browser routes and forwards requests such as /api/* to the backend service. It can also terminate TLS and apply headers or limits.
code:
Browser
  -> HTTPS reverse proxy
     /       -> React assets
     /api/*  -> Spring Boot
delivery: A reverse proxy gives me a clean public boundary and can simplify TLS, routing and same-origin behavior for the browser.
followups: How do you handle SPA fallback routes?
traps: Do not forward sensitive headers or trust proxy metadata without configuring trusted proxies correctly.

title: Handling CORS in development and production
what: CORS controls which browser origins can make cross-origin requests to an API.
how: Spring Security or the application config allows only required origins, methods and headers. In production, same-origin deployment through a reverse proxy can reduce cross-origin complexity.
code:
Development
http://localhost:5173 -> API

Production
https://app.example.com -> API
delivery: I configure CORS for the actual browser origins and avoid using a wildcard with credentials. CORS is a browser policy, not an authentication mechanism.
traps: Do not use Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * together with credentialed requests.

title: Rate limiting a public full-stack API
what: Rate limiting protects APIs from abuse, accidental overload and some automated attacks.
how: Apply limits at the edge and/or application layer based on IP, identity, API key or operation. Return a clear 429 response and make the frontend handle it gracefully.
code:
Too many requests
-> 429 Too Many Requests
-> Retry-After: 30
delivery: I use rate limits as one layer of resilience and security. The exact key and limit depend on whether the endpoint is public, authenticated or business-critical.
followups: How do you handle distributed counters?
traps: Do not apply one global limit without considering different endpoint costs.

title: Correlation IDs from browser to Spring Boot
what: A correlation or trace identifier lets engineers connect a user-visible failure with backend logs and downstream activity.
how: A trace context is propagated from the browser or edge through Spring Boot and downstream services. Logs include the identifier and telemetry tools use it to reconstruct the request path.
code:
Browser
  trace=abc123
  -> Gateway
  -> Spring Boot
  -> downstream service
delivery: I want one request to be traceable across boundaries. That turns a frontend error from an isolated symptom into a path through the system.
followups: What data should not go into a trace?
traps: Do not place tokens, passwords or personal data into correlation IDs.

title: Health checks and readiness for a full-stack deployment
what: A deployment platform needs to distinguish a process that is alive from one that is ready to receive traffic.
how: Spring Boot exposes liveness and readiness information appropriate to the environment. The frontend deployment is considered ready only after its assets and required configuration are available.
code:
Liveness -> process is running
Readiness -> safe to receive traffic
delivery: I separate liveness from readiness so an instance can restart when unhealthy without receiving traffic before its dependencies and initialization are ready.
followups: How do rolling deployments use readiness?
traps: Do not make liveness fail for every transient downstream dependency.

title: CI/CD pipeline for React and Spring Boot
what: A full-stack pipeline builds, tests, scans and packages frontend and backend artifacts before deployment.
how: Run Java tests and build, frontend lint/tests/build, security checks, container or artifact creation, then deploy through controlled environments with rollback capability.
code:
Commit
 -> test -> scan -> build React
 -> test -> build Spring Boot
 -> package -> deploy -> verify
delivery: I want CI to catch contract, test and security failures before deployment. CD should make releases repeatable and observable rather than manual sequences of commands.
followups: How do you manage database migrations in CI?
traps: Do not make production deployment depend on an engineer's laptop state.

title: End-to-end feature rollout with backward compatibility
what: Safe full-stack releases often require old and new frontend/backend versions to coexist temporarily.
how: Deploy additive backend support first, release the new frontend, monitor usage and errors, then remove obsolete compatibility paths after all active clients have migrated.
code:
1. Add compatible API
2. Deploy backend
3. Deploy React
4. Monitor
5. Remove old contract later
delivery: I separate compatibility from cleanup. The compatibility window is what lets frontend and backend deployments move independently without breaking active users.
followups: How do you detect old clients?
traps: Do not remove the old contract in the same deployment that introduces the new frontend.

title: End-to-end full-stack feature checklist
what: A production-ready feature needs more than working UI and API code.
how: Review user flow, API contract, validation, authorization, persistence, concurrency, error states, observability, testing, deployment, rollback and documentation before release.
code:
UI -> API -> business rules -> DB
   + security + tests + telemetry + deployment
delivery: Before calling a full-stack feature production-ready, I verify behavior at every boundary and especially the failure paths. Happy-path functionality is only one part of readiness.
followups: What would you monitor after release?
How do you prove authorization works?
traps: Do not define production readiness as 'the happy path works'.
